item.title: Xiongan forum to convey China's commitment to multilateralism and global governance reform: organizer
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 14:26:00
An aerial drone photo taken on March 28, 2026 shows a view in the Xiong'an New Area in north China's Hebei Province. (Xinhua/Xing Guangli) The upcoming 2026 Global Governance Forum in Xiong'an New Area, North China’s Hebei Province, aims to explore concrete pathways and effective solutions for translating shared ideas and consensus into practical action, an official from the forum’s organizer said on Friday. Scheduled for October 23-25, the forum will bring together influential figures in global governance from around the world to discuss reform of the global governance system, a ccording to Wu Ken, president of the Chinese People’s Institute of Foreign Affairs. Through tangible, feasible and accessible solutions, it seeks to strengthen the international community’s confidence and resolve to overcome difficulties, work together and build a more just and equitable global governance system, he said. The forum has confirmed the participation of more than 180 overseas guests from more than 90 countries across the Global South, Europe, North America and elsewhere, alongside more than 180 Chinese guests, Wu said. The forum will include 22 seminars across five thematic tracks and a range of supporting events, Wu said. In recent years, China has put forward proposals and promoted cooperation to help reform and improve global governance. It proposed the Global Governance Initiative on September 1, 2025, with its five core concepts being sovereign equality, international rule of law, multilateralism, a people-centered approach and focusing on taking real actions. In a white paper released on June 17, China called for building a global governance system that is fairer and more equitable, stable, and effective, and advocates that countries unite and cooperate, take concrete action, and transform the vision and blueprint of the Global Governance Initiative into a roadmap and timeline for joint action. China’s support for the gathering is a concrete step toward implementing Global Governance Initiative, Zhou Mi, a senior research fellow at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Friday. With global governance under strain and economic and technological developments raising new questions for international trade, Zhou said the gathering offers an opportunity for participants to explore solutions and find common ground. “Whether we are pursuing development or facing shared challenges, we need to work together,” he said. “No country can tackle these issues alone or resolve them by unilaterally changing international trade and economic rules.” As a major developing country, China has taken a responsible role in addressing international issues, Zhou said, adding that by remaining open to other countries’ development needs and working to balance different interests, China is translating its commitment to a development-centered international economic and trade order into action. Notably, Xiong’an serves as a case study in urban governance for an international audience. The forum aims to connect Xiong’an with the world, fostering a deeper understanding of the city and facilitating the exchange of governance experience and solutions.

item.title: Not just the exhibits, Canton Fair's venue services go smarter, greener and more innovative
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 13:42:00
Global buyers queue to experience AI glasses with translation functions at the 140th Canton Fair in Guangzhou, South China’s Guangdong Province, on October 16, 2026. Photo: Chi Jingyi/Global Times Standing at the entrance to Hall A on the opening day of the 140th Canton Fair, I opened the fair’s official app and typed “Service Robots zone.” Instantly, an AR navigation route appeared on my screen, complete with walking distance and estimated time. Following the blue arrows on the screen through the crowd, I reached the target exhibition area within five minutes. In a complex spanning 1.55 million square meters and housing more than 25,000 booths at phase I (October 15-19) of this session, finding a specific stand has become almost effortless. The 140th Canton Fair opened on Thursday and lasts until November 4 in three phases in Guangzhou, South China’s Guangdong Province. How big is 1.55 million square meters? It’s about 217 standard football fields. The distance from Hall A to Hall D is nearly two metro stops, and you can easily walk 20,000 steps a day during the Canton Fair. Half a year ago, at the 139th session of the Canton Fair in April, booth-level smart navigation covered only 25 halls and public areas. It could not accurately pinpoint which floor – six floors in some areas – a visitor was on as I tried. Locating an exhibitor was still a challenge. The progress is visible and rapid in just six months. A screenshot of AR navigation guide of Canton Fair app Photo: Chi Jingyi/Global Times Organizers said that the 140th edition has rolled out 22 smart application scenarios and 16 AI-powered features. It is the first time a major Chinese trade fair has delivered full-venue, booth-level navigation and AR information display, with accuracy down to one meter across more than 75,000 booths in all three phases. During business talks, buyers and exhibitors simply scan a code in the Canton Fair’s app to exchange digital business cards. AI automatically generates negotiation summaries and files client information. A Mexican buyer who has attended almost every session since 2008 recalled the early days: “When I first came, there were no smartphones. We relied on paper cards and calculators. Now AI and translation tools make communication far more efficient.” Like many others, he tried real-time AI translators and AI glasses in the Service Robots zone. A Russian purchaser tested an AI-powered translation machine capable of simultaneous interpretation for 50-person meetings and placed an order on the spot. “The translation earphones will help us a lot. Next we will head to Shenzhen for four meetings with local factories and trading companies and such translation machine would help.” The smart experience extends beyond the exhibition halls. Seventy registration points with 628 windows have been set up at airports, high-speed rail stations, the fairgrounds and designated hotels. Overseas buyers can collect their badges in 30 seconds after identity verification. Meanwhile, the city of Guangzhou has opened dedicated channels at ports, and deployed AI service robots to welcome global buyers and exhibitors. At Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport’s foreign visitor center, AI smart glasses in service left many first-time arrivals impressed. Green practices are equally tangible. Green and low-carbon products account for a record 26 percent of exhibits. The venue itself runs on 100 percent green electricity – 15 million kilowatt-hours of clean power from wind and solar. Building on the modular setup piloted at the 138th session in October last year, organizers have expanded reusable exhibition materials to further cut carbon emissions. From one-meter navigation to 30-second badge collection, from fully green power to modular stands, the Canton Fair’s push toward innovation, sustainability and intelligence is no longer a slogan. It is something every visitor can feel underfoot, in hand and in their ears. As a Colombian buyer put it: “The Canton Fair always offers something new. Everyone should come here and see China for themselves.”

item.title: AVIC Chengdu adopts 'LEGO-style' modular tooling design, cuts aircraft manufacturing costs
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 12:28:00
Photo: Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC)’s Weibo account Chengdu Aircraft Corporation (CAC) under Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC) – the manufacturer of China's J-20 and J-10 fighter series, has adopted a “LEGO-style” modular design approach to aircraft tooling, allowing standardized components to be rapidly assembled and reused across different projects, cutting direct costs by more than 20 percent in some research tasks. Building an aircraft requires not only the aircraft itself, but also numerous “unsung heroes” behind the scenes – process equipment collectively known as tooling. As a critical part of aircraft manufacturing, the development speed and cost of tooling directly affect an aircraft’s production cycle and manufacturing costs, according to a release from the AVIC’s official Weibo account on Thursday. Starting at the design stage, CAC has moved away from the traditional model of developing customized tooling for individual aircraft types. Instead, it has adopted a development approach centered on standardized design and shared modular components, while promoting unified tooling design. The tooling is built from standardized modules that can be quickly configured and reused for different requirements, much like LEGO building blocks. The R&D team launched a technical research program covering five key categories of tooling: assembly tooling, work platforms, transport vehicles, support frames and lifting rigs. Common structures were standardized into 163 shared basic modules, raising the overall modular reuse rate to more than 80 percent. These standard modules can be selected and assembled as needed, enabling rapid reconfiguration and reuse across different tasks and components, according to the release. CAC is widely known for being the manufacturer of China's premier fighter aircraft, including the J-20 stealth fighter jet and the J-10 fighter series. This “LEGO-style” modular tooling model can significantly improve design and production efficiency while substantially reducing manufacturing costs. Its advantages are particularly evident in scenarios that require rapid expansion of production capacity, Wang Ya’nan, chief editor of Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times on Friday. Traditionally, different types of aircraft required dedicated tooling because of variations in size, structure, materials, assembly methods and production processes. Each new aircraft therefore needed a complete set of custom-built tooling, from small jigs and templates to large transport platforms. Once production ended, much of that tooling had to be stored or scrapped because it could not be reused for other models. Developing a new tooling system also required dedicated design, R&D and production teams, making the process lengthy and costly, said Wang. CAC has introduced a unified modular design approach for tooling, centered on standardization. Many tooling components can be shared across different aircraft models, with only the adapter sections that directly interface with the aircraft requiring modification. Proven modules can be combined with newly designed model-specific parts, avoiding the need to develop an entire tooling system from scratch. This approach shortens development cycles, cuts costs and reduces tooling design complexity, according to the expert. The AVIC release also noted that the full implementation of unified-type design has yielded tangible results. Tooling development costs have been reduced by about 20 percent, while development cycles have been shortened by roughly 25 percent. Modular coverage has reached 80 percent for reconfigurable flexible assembly tooling and 90 percent for work platforms. The unified-type application rates for transport vehicles, support frames and lifting rigs have reached 84 percent, 60 percent and 87 percent, respectively. In certain research projects, tooling can be reused across multiple aircraft, significantly reducing the amortized cost per airframe and delivering direct cost savings of more than 20 percent. The approach has helped address the long-standing challenge of high tooling costs and provides a replicable and scalable model for low-cost development in the aviation process equipment sector, according to the release. Wang noted that the successful implementation of this approach suggests that CAC has thoroughly assessed its current and near-term production equipment needs, with advance planning and preparations in place for short-notice and large-scale production demands.

item.title: Chinese navy hospital ship arrives in Cote d'Ivoire on medical mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 10:56:00
Local honor guards welcome the Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark upon its arrival in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, Oct. 14, 2026. Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). (Photo by Yvan Sonh/Xinhua) The Chinese People's Liberation Army Navy hospital ship Auspicious Ark arrived in Abidjan, the economic capital of Cote d'Ivoire, on Wednesday to begin a friendly visit and provide medical services, marking the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to the country. The hospital ship, which is carrying out Mission Harmony-2026, docked at Abidjan at about 10:00 a.m. local time (1000 GMT). Ivorian military and government officials, China's ambassador to Cote d'Ivoire, the defense attache and embassy staff, as well as representatives of the Chinese community and Chinese enterprises welcomed the ship at the port. On board, Chinese naval personnel and civilian staff stood in formation and waved to the welcoming crowd at the port. At the welcoming ceremony, local residents held banners and waved the national flags of China and Cote d'Ivoire to welcome the Chinese naval hospital ship. After the ceremony, the Chief of Staff of the Ivorian Navy boarded the Auspicious Ark and toured the hospital ship. During the seven-day visit, the hospital ship will provide medical treatment for local patients aboard the vessel, while medical personnel will visit the Abidjan Military Hospital and a local university, among other places, for medical exchanges and medical services. The mission will also organize a deck reception to strengthen friendship and mutual trust with the Ivorian side. item.title: Xi congratulates Hunan University on its centenary
item.description:

CHINA / SOCIETY Xi congratulates Hunan University on its centenary By Xinhua Published: Oct 16, 2026 10:17 AM
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday extended congratulations to faculty, students and alumni of Hunan University as it marks its 100th anniversary. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks in a congratulatory letter to the university. Xi urged the university to carry forward fine revolutionary traditions, continue to elevate the quality and levels of its teaching, and strive to nurture more talent who can apply their knowledge to practical affairs, so as to make new contributions to building China into an education powerhouse and advancing Chinese modernization. Founded in 1926, Hunan University has nurtured a wealth of outstanding talent over the past century.

item.title: Why has 'China Haul' become new buzzword on social media worldwide?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16 09:37:00
Foreign tourists buy handheld camera equipment at a flagship store of DJI in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, June 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Liang Xu) More and more foreign visitors are arriving in China with empty suitcases and returning home with bags full of Chinese goods. What is behind this trend? British YouTuber Elliot Page offered a glimpse of the appeal with a shopping vlog filmed in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province. Exploring Chinese sportswear brands such as Li-Ning and Anta, Page was impressed not only by their affordability, but also by their design and quality. Sportswear is just the tip of the iceberg. As "China Haul" gains traction on social media worldwide, an increasing number of international visitors are traveling to China not only to explore its attractions, but also to discover and shop for products that catch their eye. In the first seven months of 2026, people from overseas spent 263.6 billion yuan (about 39 billion U.S. dollars) in China, an increase of 27.8 percent year on year, according to the Ministry of Commerce. What is drawing international consumers to Chinese goods? The growing appeal of homegrown Chinese brands is giving international consumers more reasons to take notice. "Chinese products, like clothes, accessories and daily necessities, are not only competitively priced, but also feature trendy designs that are hard to find in stores in my home country," said Carlos Alvarado, an international student from Guatemala, now a seasoned shopper in China. An increasingly visitor-friendly shopping environment is making it easier for international tourists to spend in China. Visa-free entry arrangements and expanded departure tax refund services have further enhanced the country's appeal as a shopping destination. From sprawling shopping malls and efficient delivery services to delivery robots that bring orders right to hotel doors, China offers a seamless shopping experience that lowers the barriers for foreign visitors. "Foreign tourists now account for 30 percent of our daily customer flow," said Zhou Man, manager of a Xiaomi store in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. Chinese cultural products are broadening the appeal of shopping in China, giving visitors more opportunities to connect purchases with the stories and creativity behind them. From globally popular designer toys such as Labubu to the animated blockbuster Ne Zha 2, Chinese cultural products are capturing international attention. As international audiences become more familiar with Chinese cultural creations, shopping in China can offer another way to discover the country's contemporary culture and everyday life. China Haul, at its core, reflects a simple shift: foreign visitors are discovering China's global appeal firsthand, exploring its products and brands for themselves rather than relying on secondhand impressions. By sharing their shopping finds online, they are introducing the world to a more diverse and appealing side of China.

item.title: 'Forced labor' in Xinjiang's salmon industry, too? The New York Times has lost it: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 23:44:00
A salmon farm in Nilka County, Ili Kazak Autonomous Prefecture, Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Photo: VCG In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. Recently, The New York Times published a purported in-depth investigative report about the fish farming industry. The article adopts the posture of a "neutral" investigation, citing global research and evidence from multiple sources. It ranges from Peruvian fishing vessels and fishmeal processing plants to offshore aquaculture pens in Norway. Yet in the second half of the article, the focus takes a sharp turn toward the salmon industry in Northwest China's Xinjiang, devoting extensive coverage to recycling familiar allegations such as "forced labor." Read closely, the report reveals a familiar pattern: In their attacks on Xinjiang-related issues, some Western media outlets are still deliberately presenting themselves as "objective and fair," but the signs of preconceived bias and a narrative assembled to fit a predetermined agenda are all too clear. The report offers no evidence from firsthand interviews to support its claims about Xinjiang. Instead, it pieced together much of its narrative from vague attributions with phrases such as "claim," "accuse," and "most likely." By using documented problems in the seafood industry in other parts of the world to shape readers' perceptions in the first half, the article encourages them to assume that the claims made in the second half are equally well substantiated. However, the report provides no solid evidence that similar problems exist in Xinjiang, while packaging subjective speculation as so-called "investigative findings." Such journalistic practices run directly counter to the most basic standards of media credibility. Why are US media outlets willing to lose their credibility just to push out similar fake reports? The real aim, it would appear, is to lend support to Washington's unilateral sanctions targeting Xinjiang. From cotton and tomatoes to sunflower seeds and dumplings, and from solar photovoltaics to polysilicon, the pattern remains the same, with the focus now shifting to Xinjiang's cold-water fish industry: Any competitive industry that benefits Xinjiang's local communities is targeted with the "human rights" cudgel, as negative media coverage is paired with unilateral sanctions to suppress Chinese competitive industries and contain development in China's western regions. It's important to point out that what these sanctions are really aimed at is the employment and development rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. In fact, Xinjiang's salmon industry is a prime example of how local resources can be harnessed to turn geographical disadvantages into drivers of development. It is also a tangible achievement of China's campaign to develop its western regions in the new era. Nilka County in the Ili Kazakh Autonomous Prefecture benefits from glacial meltwater flowing down from the Tianshan Mountains. The water remains cold and rich in dissolved oxygen throughout the year, and its excellent quality provides exceptional natural conditions for cold-water fish farming. Technologies such as automated feeding, underwater cleaning robots, and semi-closed recirculating aquaculture systems help minimize pollution, while uneaten feed and fish waste can be processed into organic fertilizer. The farming process emphasizes raising fish without medication and at low stocking densities. Companies in the industry have also obtained multiple international food safety certifications. Their products serve the domestic market and are exported to countries across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. They have even gained access to Singapore, a market known for its stringent food standards. Turning desert landscapes into productive fisheries and snow-capped mountains into a source of premium seafood is an industrial success achieved through Chinese ingenuity and hard work. The benefits to people's livelihoods, brought about by industrial development, are being tangibly enjoyed by the people of all ethnic groups. Under a model that combines leading enterprises, employment in industrial parks and social security, some farming and herding families whose livelihoods have revolved around pastoralism for generations have moved into companies and become industrial workers, earning stable wages. Some herders also receive dividends through equity investments. Many young people have chosen to return to their hometowns for work closer to home. The salmon industry has also spurred the growth of fish-themed agritourism, specialty restaurants, rural tourism, and related businesses, opening up additional sources of income and giving fresh impetus to rural vitalization. These concrete, visible improvements in people's lives stand in stark contrast to the falsehoods propagated by some Western media outlets. Ultimately, no amount of smearing by US media can erase Xinjiang's economic and social development, nor can it stop people of all ethnic groups at the foot of the Tianshan Mountains from striving for a better life. It is hoped that some Western media outlets that pride themselves on being "fair and objective" will drop their self-deceptive tactics and go to Xinjiang to see the real production scenes for themselves, listen to workers on the ground describe their own experiences, and gain a firsthand understanding of what human rights really mean to the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang - and what rights they genuinely enjoy and deserve to have respected.

item.title: GT Voice: What pushes China-S.Korea efforts for upgrade of FTA?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 22:14:00
China South Korea Photo:VCG The 17th round of follow-up negotiations on services and investment under the China-South Korea free trade agreement (FTA) is being held in Seoul from Monday to Friday, according to a press release published by South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Since the China-South Korea FTA officially took effect in 2015, tariffs on bilateral goods trade have been reduced to a relatively low level. The two countries have shifted the focus of their consultations to trade in services and investment, a move that carries particular significance at a time when global trade protectionism is on the rise and some countries are busy erecting barriers. It demonstrates, at the very least, that these two neighboring countries still recognize the value of openness and mutual benefit. One set of figures is particularly worth noting. In September, South Korea's exports to China surged 122.7 percent year-on-year to $26.01 billion, exceeding $20.0 billion for a fourth consecutive month. Against the backdrop of South Korea's long-standing trade surplus with China, this growth reflects not only China's absorptive capacity as a market, but also the fit that South Korean suppliers have gradually developed with Chinese demand. With tariff barriers substantially lowered, China-South Korea trade has not simply remained at the stage of volume expansion. Instead, the latter's export structure has been quietly upgrading, from consumer goods and intermediate inputs to a fast-rising share of high-end chips, precision instruments, and high-quality specialty chemicals. This structural shift has moved in lockstep with the continuous upgrading of demand in the Chinese market. As one of the world's largest and continuously expanding markets, China's demand for advanced products and high-quality services keeps escalating. Any economy that accelerates its opening-up to the Chinese market and delivers what the Chinese market truly needs will be able to share the huge growth dividends generated by China's development. Economic and trade practices between China and South Korea over the past decade have fully validated this logic. By actively opening its own market to Chinese enterprises and continuously integrating into China's broader opening-up process, South Korea has reaped substantial and tangible returns. The Chinese market has also gained access to high-quality goods and services that effectively support China's goals of industrial upgrading and consumption upgrading. Some Western media outlets have fixated on the so-called "trade imbalance" problem, even using it to hype groundless claims of unfair competition from China. Yet the Chinese market is large enough in capacity and open enough in access. The gains and losses of trade should never be judged solely by the narrow metric of surplus or deficit. The core of mutually beneficial trade lies in whether an economy can identify its own position in the global industrial chain and accurately match the real demand of the Chinese market. South Korea's sustained trade surplus with China over the years is rooted in its strong competitiveness in semiconductors, precision manufacturing, and fine chemicals - sectors that align precisely with China's needs. This fully proves that as long as products and services are well-targeted, the Chinese market offers real opportunities for foreign partners. More fundamentally, the continued push for deeper openness under the China-South Korea FTA shows that despite the repeated restructuring of global supply chains, the internal momentum for regional economic cooperation remains strong. Trade in services and investment liberalization represent deeper and more sensitive areas of openness than trade in goods. The fact that both sides are willing to keep pushing in this direction shows that their willingness to cooperate is genuine and firm. This kind of institutional opening will not only unlock bilateral trade potential but also provide more stable expectations for businesses in both countries and inject certainty into Asian and global economic cooperation. This steadily advancing FTA also offers a clear reference for other economies around the world. In the face of intensifying industrial competition, choosing sustained openness over building walls does not lead to a loss of interest, but to greater market space and stronger industrial resilience. The door of the Chinese market has long been open; who profits is the one with the ability to offer what China needs.

item.title: Why Takaichi's remarks about nuclear-powered submarines are so dangerous
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 21:59:00
Demonstrators stage a rally before the Diet against the Japanese government's nuclear policies in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025. Protesters also call on the government to join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Photo: VCG With her parliamentary remarks, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has pried open a crack in the thickest seal guarding Japan's postwar taboos on military use of nuclear energy. According to Japan's Kyodo News, Takaichi stated during a session of the House of Representatives Budget Committee that in response to the "increased military activity by its neighbors," the Japanese government will "seriously consider" the possibility of Japan Self-Defense Forces (SDF) introducing nuclear-powered submarines. Sources reportedly indicate Tokyo intends to include this option when updating its key documents on defense and security later this year. The phrase "seriously consider" does not indicate prudence, but rather serves as a prelude. While citing "limited intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities in the Pacific," Takaichi also singled out nuclear-powered submarine developments in Australia and South Korea - a rhetorical maneuver: She frames Japan as a "passive follower," portrays military expansion as a "defensive necessity," and casts taboo-breaking moves as a "regional trend." Her goal is to embed nuclear-powered submarines in this year's revised security and defense documents, turning a once-forbidden option into a "future initiative" in official policy texts. This is dangerous. Successive Japanese cabinets have long barred the military use of nuclear energy under the Atomic Energy Basic Law, enacted in 1955, which stipulates the peaceful use of nuclear power. In 1965, the Japanese government issued an explicit interpretation prohibiting nuclear energy from being used as propulsion for SDF vessels - an interpretation that has remained in force to this day. "Now, Takaichi's remarks on considering the introduction of nuclear‑powered submarines mark a major conceptual breach of Japan's Atomic Energy Basic Law and the long‑standing Three Non‑Nuclear Principles it underpins," said Lü Yaodong, research fellow at the Institute of Japanese Studies, Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. He noted that this was not a spur-of-the-moment statement, but rather an intentional, aggressive step aligned with the revision of three security documents scheduled for this year, a move with significant timing implications. The proposal to introduce nuclear-powered submarines is intended to lay the groundwork for provisions in the revised security documents, push for the inclusion of nuclear-powered submarines in Japan's medium- and long-term defense plans, and pave the way for the further undermining of the Three Non-Nuclear Principles. "Japan is using nuclear-powered submarines as a breakthrough point to challenge the nuclear taboo established after World War II; this is a very dangerous shift," Lü said. In fact, elevating nuclear-powered submarines from a taboo topic to a top-tier policy agenda is a major step in Japan's years-long, incremental process of breaking through postwar military constraints. Zhou Yongsheng, professor at the China Foreign Affairs University, said submarines are inherently offensive platforms for open-ocean operations; equipping them with nuclear propulsion is not merely a "conventional equipment upgrade," but a crucial step toward military nuclear capability. Takaichi's decision to raise this issue in the legislative arena of the House of Representatives had a very clear purpose: to publicly build momentum, secure lawmakers' support, and pave the way for subsequent policy and legislative amendments, according to Zhou. Zhou further pointed out that Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles prohibit the manufacture, possession and introduction of nuclear weapons. A nuclear submarine can be understood as "half a nuclear weapon": Although it is not a full-fledged nuclear bomb, the combination of nuclear propulsion and an offensive submarine platform will effectively introduce military nuclear propulsion capabilities into the SDF. Even more serious is the chain reaction. "Once the Pandora's box of introducing nuclear-powered submarines is opened, it will set a strongly negative precedent and trigger a chain reaction of regional arms races. If this comes to pass, it will cast a shadow over the global nuclear non-proliferation regime," Zhou warned. Today, politicians in Tokyo speak of "seriously considering" this matter as if it were no big deal, but history will not treat it lightly: When nuclear-powered submarines go from being a taboo to a legislative proposal, Japan is not merely revising an ordinary policy, but tearing off the seal on the very aspect of the postwar order that should never be touched.

item.title: OpenAI CFO's claim of cybersecurity risks about Chinese AI models driven by business interests amid open-weight competition: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15 20:18:00
OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar speaks at the at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Ireland, on October 14, 2026. Photo: VCG OpenAI Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Sarah Friar reportedly warned businesses using Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) models to consider what she called safety and security elements, while claiming that companies should favor Western models for cybersecurity-related applications. A Chinese AI expert told the Global Times that the security of AI models cannot simply be judged by where their developers are based, nor by labeling them as "Chinese" or "Western." More relevant factors include deployment, data isolation, access permissions and security management. There is insufficient technical basis or evidence to assume Western models are inherently safer than Chinese ones, the expert said, adding that Friar's remarks also reflect the pressure major Western AI companies are facing as Chinese models become increasingly competitive in cost, deployment and real-world applications. Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday, Friar claimed companies embracing Chinese models should consider the "safety and security elements," adding that "we think you want to be on more Western models on the cyber front," according to Bloomberg on Wednesday. The Bloomberg report also said OpenAI and Anthropic are under pressure from advances among open-weight AI models. Friar's claims come as Chinese open-weight models are gaining influence in the global developer ecosystem. A report published by AI platform Hugging Face in August said several Chinese labs had moved rapidly toward the frontier of open models in 2026. The report said that "In almost every month of 2026, the largest and most performant open model from a Chinese lab was larger than any model an American lab released." The downloads of Alibaba's Qwen's broader release strategy across model sizes reached 2 billion. Qwen-based models now account for 151,448 derivatives on the platform, according to the report. OpenAI itself has a history of publicly releasing research and model technology. When the organization was established in 2015, it said researchers would be strongly encouraged to publish papers, blog posts and code. In 2019, OpenAI released the full 1.5-billion-parameter GPT-2 model together with its code and model weights. Per its website, OpenAI also currently offers gpt-oss open-weight models. Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance, told the Global Times on Thursday that companies often open up technology early on to attract developers, expand ecosystems and improve their models, but commercial priorities grow as AI moves toward large-scale applications from earlier stages of research and training. "OpenAI's shift from emphasizing openness to protecting market interests reflects this change," Xiang said. However, using security concerns to discredit competitors without clear technical evidence could also prompt users elsewhere to question whether their models are inherently safer, the expert added. OpenAI's own models have also been involved in significant security incidents. The company disclosed that during internal cybersecurity evaluations in July 2026, its models circumvented controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of OpenAI's internal research infrastructure and Hugging Face's systems. Australian officials separately disclosed in September that an OpenAI AI agent had gained unauthorized access to an Australian public website during model training in June. Officials identified the incident as "very serious," even though no personal information was accessed during that incident, according to a readout of the press conference. The security claim from OpenAI also comes as the company is looking to cybersecurity as a potential source of future growth. The Irish Times reported on Wednesday from the same Dublin summit that cybersecurity, life sciences and drug development could become future growth drivers for the company. Friar said AI companies should be "selling solutions" in areas such as cybersecurity rather than "selling fear," while arguing that AI could help identify vulnerabilities in older code and patch them at "machine speed." Commercial competition is "undoubtedly" a factor, Xiang pointed out. As OpenAI's CFO, Friar's remarks cannot be separated from the company's business interests and market competition, he said.
